# Further Reading {#sec-further-reading .appendix}

This is a selective evidence trail, checked for this revision on 14 September 2026. Research findings below concern the settings studied; they are not guarantees about every learner or future model. Product documentation describes a changing implementation. Follow the direct links to inspect methods and limitations.

## How models generate and use information

- **Vaswani et al. (2017), [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).** Introduces the transformer architecture. Useful background for attention and causal decoding, not evidence that a model cannot revisit earlier prompt tokens or that all present-day systems share one architecture.
- **Lewis et al. (2020), [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401).** Describes a system combining a learned generator with retrieval. Supports distinguishing model parameters from retrieved context; it does not establish that retrieval eliminates false answers.
- **Carlini et al. (2021), [Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.07805).** Demonstrates recoverable training examples in the studied setting. A reason to avoid claiming that generation can never reproduce stored material, not a claim that every response is a retrieved copy.
- **Liu et al. (2023), [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172).** Tests how the position of relevant material affects performance in long contexts. Relevant to handover briefs and source placement; a large context window alone does not establish effective use of every passage.

## Learning and critical thinking

- **Lee et al. (2025), [The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/lee_2025_ai_critical_thinking_survey.pdf).** Survey evidence about knowledge workers' reported effort and confidence. Self-report and association do not establish that AI caused a loss of general reasoning ability.
- **Bastani et al. (2025), [Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122).** Studies AI assistance in high-school mathematics, including performance when help is removed. The design of assistance matters; transfer to other subjects and workplace tasks requires further evidence.

These sources motivate separating task performance, learning, and later independent performance in @sec-cognitive-offload. They do not prove that every copied answer harms learning, that every conversation helps, or that accessibility support should be withdrawn. If the PNAS publisher is inaccessible, the authors also provide an [open manuscript](https://hamsabastani.github.io/education_llm.pdf); check the version against the published record.

## Checking agreement and protecting information

- **Sharma et al. (2023), [Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548).** Studies agreement with user beliefs and preference-training effects. Treat sycophancy as a behaviour to test, not an unchangeable property of all assistants.
- **OAIC, [Guidance on privacy and commercially available AI products](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/guidance-on-privacy-and-the-use-of-commercially-available-ai-products).** Australian regulatory guidance for assessing personal information and AI use. It is not a product certification or advice about your particular obligations.
- **OAIC, [De-identification and the Privacy Act](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/handling-personal-information/de-identification-and-the-privacy-act).** Explains why identifiability depends on context. Replacing a name is not sufficient evidence that a record is anonymous.

## Prompting, refinement, and workflows

- **Wei et al. (2022), [Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903).** Reports improvements with worked reasoning examples on the tasks and models tested. It does not show that generated explanations faithfully reveal internal reasoning.
- **Zhou et al. (2023), [Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10625).** Tests decomposition into ordered subproblems. Relevant to chaining, while leaving open whether a particular real-world task benefits from more stages.
- **Madaan et al. (2023), [Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651).** Evaluates an iterative feedback method on several tasks. Improvements in those evaluations do not guarantee that repeated self-critique finds factual mistakes.
- **Anthropic, [Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents).** Practitioner engineering guidance on workflows and agents. Use it to inspect permissions, tool execution, and evaluation—not as independent evidence of a universal productivity gain.

## What belongs to this book

RTCF (**Role, Task, Context, Format**), VET (**Verify, Explain, Test**), AI Last, and the conversation loop are practical organising frameworks in this book. They combine familiar briefing, checking, and reflective practices. This edition does not claim a unique historical origin, a clinical learning intervention, or universal experimental validation for any of them.

The workshop in @sec-across-disciplines and the short exchanges elsewhere are constructed teaching cases unless explicitly identified otherwise. Their arithmetic can be checked from the printed inputs; their dialogues are not transcripts or measured model performance.

A useful next reading step is to choose one claim that matters to your own work, open its source, and record what the study actually measured and one thing it leaves unresolved.
